reference_items.subject: Mathematics
reference_items.stem: One of these angles is a right angle. Which one?
reference_items.figure_description:
Four angles labeled A, B, C, and D:
- Option A shows two connected line segments meeting at an apex pointing upward, one segment sloping down to the left at roughly 45° and the other sloping down to the right at roughly 45°.
- Option B shows two connected line segments meeting at a bottom vertex, one extending nearly vertically upward and the other slanting upward and to the right, forming an angle of approximately 25°.
- Option C shows two connected line segments meeting at a top vertex, one extending vertically downward and the other slanting downward and to the left, forming an angle of approximately 20°.
- Option D shows two connected line segments meeting at a bottom vertex, one slanting downward to the right and the other extending horizontally to the right, forming an angle of approximately 120°.
reference_items.calibration: Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 2007 and 2011 fourth-grade mathematics data.

reference_items.subject: Mathematics
reference_items.stem:
Jill had a rectangular piece of paper.

[Image: A rectangle divided horizontally into two equal halves by a dotted line]

She cut her paper along the dotted line and made an L shape like this.

[Image: An L-shaped figure made of two rectangular strips]

Which of these statements is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The area of the L shape is greater than the area of the rectangle.

options.label: B
options.text: The area of the L shape is equal to the area of the rectangle.

options.label: C
options.text: The area of the L shape is less than the area of the rectangle.

options.label: D
options.text: You cannot work out which area is greater without measuring.

reference_items.figure_description:
The first figure shows a horizontal rectangle with a dashed horizontal line dividing it into two equal top and bottom halves.

The second figure shows an L shape made from the two halves: one vertical rectangular strip on the left and one horizontal rectangular strip at the bottom right, joined along part of their edges at a right angle.
reference_items.calibration: Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 2003 data, 2007 bridging data, and 2007 data (fourth-grade mathematics).

reference_items.figure_description:
A 10 by 10 grid of identical square units. Two line segments forming a 90° angle are drawn on the grid:
- The corner vertex shared by both segments is at grid intersection (2, 5), counting from the bottom-left corner at (0, 0).
- The shorter segment extends diagonally up and right across 2 squares, ending at grid intersection (4, 7).
- The longer segment extends diagonally down and right across 4 squares, ending at grid intersection (6, 1).

reference_items.subject: Mathematics
reference_items.stem:
[Image: four angles varied in size and labeled P, Q, R, and S from left to right.]

In which of the following are the angles ordered by size, from least to greatest?
reference_items.figure_description:
Four angles are shown side by side, labeled from left to right as P, Q, R, and S. Each angle has a horizontal ray pointing to the right, a second ray extending from the left endpoint, and a curved arc indicating the angle between the two rays:
- Angle P is an acute angle opening upward and to the right at approximately 45°.
- Angle Q is an obtuse angle opening upward and to the left at approximately 120°.
- Angle R is a right angle (90°) formed with a vertical ray extending straight up.
- Angle S is an acute angle opening upward and to the right at approximately 30°, smaller than angle P.
reference_items.calibration: Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 2007 and 2011 fourth-grade mathematics data.

reference_items.subject: Mathematics
reference_items.stem:
Sam said that 1/3 of a pie is less than 1/4 of the same pie.

Is Sam correct? ____

Use the circles below to show why this is so.

[Image: Two circles]

Shade in 1/3 of this circle

Shade in 1/4 of this circle

descriptors: NO. Both circles are correctly partitioned.
NO. No partitioning is shown.
NO. Only one of the circles correctly partitioned.
NO. Other incorrect ways of partitioning.
YES, or there is no conclusion stated. Both circles are correctly partitioned.
Other partial.
YES. No partitioning is shown.
YES. The part representing 1/3 is made consistently smaller than the part representing 1/4.
YES. Other responses where one or both of the circles partitioned into 3 and/or 4 parts.
Other incorrect.

reference_items.scoring_notes: Note: The partition of circles has priority over shading. This is reflected in the scoring guide below.
reference_items.figure_description: Two identical, empty circles are shown side by side. Below the left circle is the text "Shade in 1/3 of this circle" with 1/3 written as a vertical fraction. Below the right circle is the text "Shade in 1/4 of this circle" with 1/4 written as a vertical fraction.

reference_items.figure_description:
An 8 by 8 grid of square cells with a vertical dashed line of symmetry running along the central vertical grid line (between the 4th and 5th columns from the left).
To the right of the dashed line is a six-sided polygon with vertices at grid intersections (with column lines 0 to 8 from left to right, and row lines 0 to 8 from top to bottom):
- (column 4, row 3) on the dashed line
- (column 5, row 2)
- (column 6, row 4)
- (column 7, row 4)
- (column 7, row 6)
- (column 4, row 5) on the dashed line

The edges of the polygon connect these vertices in sequence:
- A straight segment from (4, 3) up and right to (5, 2)
- A segment from (5, 2) down and right to (6, 4)
- A horizontal segment from (6, 4) to (7, 4)
- A vertical segment from (7, 4) down to (7, 6)
- A slanted segment from (7, 6) up and left to (4, 5)
- A vertical segment of length 2 along the dashed line from (4, 5) up to (4, 3)

reference_items.subject: Mathematics
reference_items.stem:
[Image: Three arrangements of 3 tiles labeled Rita, Ina, and Lana]

Rita, Ina, and Lana take turns arranging 3 tiles. Each arranges the tiles in a different shape as shown above. Which of the following is true about the area of the shapes?

options.label: A
options.text: Rita’s shape has a greater area than the others.

options.label: B
options.text: Ina’s shape has a greater area than the others.

options.label: C
options.text: Lana’s shape has a greater area than the others.

options.label: D
options.text: All of the shapes have the same area.

reference_items.figure_description:
Three arrangements of three tiles each, labeled "Rita", "Ina", and "Lana":
- Rita: Two squares are placed side by side horizontally, sharing a vertical edge. A triangle sits on top of the left square, with its base along the top edge of that square and its apex pointing upward.
- Ina: A square sits at the top with horizontal top and bottom edges. Attached below it is a triangle sharing the square's bottom horizontal edge and pointing downward. Attached to the lower-right edge of the triangle is a second square, tilted diagonally downward and to the right.
- Lana: Two squares are placed side by side horizontally, sharing a vertical edge. Attached to the right vertical edge of the right square is a triangle pointing to the right.
reference_items.calibration: Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 2003 data, 2007 bridging data, and 2007 data (fourth-grade mathematics).

reference_items.figure_description:
A grid measuring 8 squares wide and 6 squares high. At the bottom right of the grid, a single square cell is indicated with dimension arrows showing a width of '1 cm' and a height of '1 cm'. An incomplete polygon is drawn with heavy black lines on the grid intersections:
- A horizontal segment 4 units long on the 1st horizontal line from the top, extending from column 1 to column 5 (where grid lines are numbered 0 to 8 horizontally, and 0 to 6 vertically).
- From the point (1, 1), a diagonal segment runs down and right 2 units horizontally and 2 units vertically to (3, 3).
- From (3, 3), a vertical segment runs down 2 units to (3, 5).
- From (3, 5), a horizontal segment runs right 2 units to (5, 5).
The points (5, 1) and (5, 5) are currently open endpoints.

slope.instructions: TIMSS scaled this 1-point item with the two-parameter logistic (2PL) model, which TIMSS uses for constructed-response items worth 1 point, in the calibration "Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 2007 and 2011 fourth-grade mathematics data". What is the item's slope (discrimination) parameter a? A higher a means that the item separates students of lower and higher mathematics ability more sharply. Choose the value closest to it. The state also lists reference items: the calibrated TIMSS items of the same grade most similar to this one (never the item itself or its other parts), most similar first, with their percent correct and their calibrated parameters, each on the scale of its own calibration. Use them to place this item.

location.instructions: TIMSS scaled this 1-point item with the two-parameter logistic (2PL) model, which TIMSS uses for constructed-response items worth 1 point, in the calibration "Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 2007 and 2011 fourth-grade mathematics data". What is the item's location (difficulty) parameter b? b is on a logit scale on which the students of the calibration average about 0; a higher b means a harder item. Choose the value closest to it. The state also lists reference items: the calibrated TIMSS items of the same grade most similar to this one (never the item itself or its other parts), most similar first, with their percent correct and their calibrated parameters, each on the scale of its own calibration. Use them to place this item.
